passages.title: A Youth Environmentalist: Melati Wijsen
passages.text:
Melati Wijsen is an Indonesian environmental activist known for helping start a campaign to reduce plastic bags in Bali. As a student, she became concerned about the amount of plastic waste found in the environment. Together with her younger sister, she helped build a youth-led movement that encouraged people to think differently about single-use plastic.

Environmental campaigns often combine public education with practical action. Volunteers may speak at schools, organise clean-ups, share information online, or ask local leaders and businesses to support changes. These activities do not solve every environmental problem immediately, but they can help people understand an issue and take part in a response.

A campaign also needs persistence. Some people may agree with its goal but find it difficult to change daily habits. Others may doubt whether individual actions make a difference. Campaigners therefore need to explain the problem clearly, listen to concerns, and show realistic steps people can take. Cooperation with communities and decision-makers can help turn awareness into action.

Wijsen's work is an example of young people contributing to environmental discussions. It does not mean that one person can fix every problem alone. Instead, it shows how an idea can grow when people communicate, organise, and keep working toward a shared goal.

passages.title: Raja Ampat: Islands, Reefs, and Marine Life
passages.text:
Raja Ampat is an island group in Southwest Papua, Indonesia. Its landscape includes green islands, clear coastal waters, reefs, and sheltered bays. The area is widely known for its marine biodiversity, which attracts divers, researchers, and visitors interested in nature. However, the beauty of the sea depends on the health of the habitats beneath the surface.

Coral reefs provide places where many marine organisms can feed, hide, and reproduce. Reefs are living systems, not underwater decorations. They can be damaged by careless boat anchoring, litter, and visitors who touch or stand on coral. Even when damage looks small, repeated contact can affect fragile organisms.

Visitors can reduce their impact by following local guidance, using designated mooring areas, taking rubbish away, and choosing operators who explain responsible practices. They should also avoid buying products made from protected wildlife. These actions do not remove every pressure on the environment, but they can prevent some avoidable harm.

Raja Ampat's natural appeal is connected to a responsibility. Tourism can support local livelihoods, yet it must be managed carefully so that the environment remains valuable for residents and future visitors. Respectful travel means enjoying the landscape without treating it as a resource that can be used without limits.

passages.title: A School Trip to a Mangrove Learning Center
passages.text:
Last Friday, my class visited a mangrove learning center near the coast. Before the trip, our teacher told us to bring notebooks, wear comfortable shoes, and stay with our groups. I thought we would only walk along the wooden path, but the guide had prepared several activities.

First, we listened to a short explanation about mangrove roots and the animals that live among them. Then, we walked to a viewing platform and wrote down three things we noticed. I saw small crabs moving through the mud and birds resting in the trees. The guide reminded us not to collect plants or disturb the animals.

After that, each group examined pictures showing how rubbish can travel from streets into rivers and then to the sea. Our group had to suggest two ways to prevent this. We suggested using rubbish bins properly and reducing single-use packaging. One student wanted to pick up a piece of litter near the water, but the guide asked us to leave it because the area was muddy and unsafe.

At the end of the visit, we shared our ideas and returned to school. I enjoyed the trip because we learned outdoors, but I also understood why visitors need to follow safety instructions.

passages.title: What I Learned from a Practice Job Interview
passages.text:
Our school career club organised a practice job interview to help students prepare for life after graduation. I signed up because I wanted to know how an interview felt before applying for a real position. I prepared a short introduction, but I did not practise answering questions about teamwork or mistakes.

At first, I spoke too quickly and gave a long answer when the interviewer asked me to describe a time I solved a problem. I started telling the whole story instead of explaining what I had done. The volunteer interviewer listened and then suggested that I focus on the situation, my action, and the result.

We tried the question again. This time, I explained how I had helped organise a class presentation after two group members were absent. I described dividing the remaining tasks and checking the slides before the deadline. My answer was shorter and easier to follow. The interviewer also advised me to pause briefly before answering and ask for clarification if a question was unclear.

After the session, I wrote down the feedback and chose two questions to practise at home. I realised that preparation is not about memorising perfect sentences. It is about selecting relevant examples and explaining them clearly. I still felt nervous, but I left with a practical plan for improving.
hints: the advice about structuring an answer

passages.title: The Legend of Roro Jonggrang
passages.text:
In a well-known Javanese legend, Bandung Bondowoso wanted to marry Roro Jonggrang after defeating her father's kingdom. Roro Jonggrang did not want to marry him, so she set a difficult condition: he had to build a thousand temples in one night. She hoped the task would be impossible to complete before dawn.

Bandung Bondowoso called on supernatural helpers, and the construction began. As the night passed, the temples rose quickly. Roro Jonggrang became afraid that he would finish, so she asked the women of the village to pound rice and create a bright glow in the east. The sounds and light made it seem as if morning had arrived.

The helpers stopped working, believing dawn had come. When Bandung Bondowoso discovered the trick, he was furious. In this version of the story, he cursed Roro Jonggrang, turning her into a stone statue to complete the number of temples. The tale is traditionally associated with the Prambanan temple complex, although the story itself is a legend rather than a verified account of the site's history.

The story is often remembered for its challenge, deception, and unhappy ending. Retellings may vary in some details, but the central conflict remains: Roro Jonggrang tries to escape a marriage by setting a task that she believes cannot be completed.
hints: how she made it seem like dawn

passages.title: The Story of Keong Mas
passages.text:
In a commonly told version of the Indonesian folktale Keong Mas, a princess is changed into a golden snail because of jealousy and magic. The details differ among retellings, but the story often follows a princess who is separated from her family and must wait for help before she can return to her human form.

After the transformation, the golden snail is found near a river and taken home by an older woman. The woman places it in a safe container and continues her daily work. She later notices something unusual: whenever she returns home, the room is tidy and food has been prepared. She does not know who has done these tasks.

One day, the woman decides to stay nearby and observe. She discovers that the golden snail has become a princess who quietly prepares the food before returning to the container. The woman treats her kindly and does not reveal her secret to others. In time, the spell is broken in the version being told, and the princess can return to her former life.

The tale uses the golden snail as a sign of hidden identity and unexpected kindness. It should be read as folklore, not as a report of a real transformation. Because the story has several versions, names, causes of the spell, and the ending may differ depending on the storyteller or source.

passages.title: How to Make a Reusable Shopping Bag from an Old T-shirt
passages.text:
An old T-shirt can become a simple shopping bag with only a few materials. This activity is useful when the shirt is still clean but is no longer worn. Ask permission before using a shirt that belongs to someone else, and choose one without large holes.

First, lay the shirt flat on a table and cut off the sleeves. Cut a wider opening around the neck to make the top of the bag. If you want the bag to have a neat shape, ask an adult to help mark the cutting lines before you begin.

Next, turn the shirt inside out. Cut short strips along the bottom edge, making sure the strips are similar in size. Tie each front strip to the matching strip at the back. Pull the knots gently to check that the bottom is closed. If there are gaps, tie the nearby strips again so small items are less likely to fall out.

Finally, turn the bag right side out and check the handles and bottom. Carry a few light items first to test it before using it for heavier shopping. The bag may not last forever, but reusing a shirt can give the material another purpose and reduce the need for a new bag.

passages.title: How to Write a Clear Email to Ask for Information
passages.text:
A clear email helps the reader understand what you need without searching through a long message. Before writing, make sure you know who should receive the email and what information you want to ask for.

First, write a short subject line that explains the purpose, such as “Question About the English Club Schedule.” Begin with a polite greeting and use the recipient's name or role if you know it. Avoid starting with a message that has no greeting or subject, because the reader may not immediately understand its purpose.

Next, introduce yourself briefly if the recipient may not know you. State your question directly and include any details needed to answer it. For example, if you are asking about a club meeting, mention the club and the date you mean. Keep the message focused instead of adding unrelated questions in the same paragraph.

Finally, thank the reader, close politely, and include your name. Before sending, check spelling, dates, and attachments. Read the email once as if you were the recipient: can you understand the request quickly? A short, organised message is usually more helpful than a long email with missing details.
hints: the purpose of the subject line

passages.title: Should Schools Replace Some Printed Materials with Digital Ones?
passages.text:
Schools should replace some printed materials with digital versions when the change genuinely helps learning. Digital files can be updated without printing a new copy, and students may be able to access them on devices they already use. However, replacing every printed resource would not be fair or practical for every learner.

One advantage is flexibility. Teachers can correct an error in a shared file, add a useful link, or provide a readable copy without distributing a new stack of paper. Students who have suitable devices may also carry several resources without bringing heavy folders. These benefits are strongest when files are organised and easy to access.

There are also limits. Not every student has a reliable device, enough data, or a stable internet connection at home. Long reading tasks may be more comfortable on paper for some learners, and screens can introduce distractions when notifications appear. A digital system also needs technical support and clear rules for access.

For these reasons, schools should use a mixed approach. Digital materials are useful for updates and flexible access, while printed copies remain important when students need them. The goal should be to choose the format that supports the task and includes learners, rather than treating one format as automatically better in every situation.

passages.title: Should Students Have Homework-Free Weekends?
passages.text:
Students need time to study, but they also need rest, family time, and opportunities to enjoy activities outside school. For this reason, schools should consider limiting weekend homework rather than expecting students to complete large amounts every Saturday and Sunday.

A lighter weekend workload can help students recover after a busy school week. Rest gives them time to sleep properly, spend time with family, exercise, or pursue hobbies. Students who return to school less exhausted may find it easier to pay attention and participate in lessons. A break can also help them approach difficult tasks with a clearer mind.

However, some homework can be useful. Short reading tasks, reviewing key notes, or preparing for an upcoming project may help students remember what they have learned. The problem is not every assignment; it is the amount and timing. Several long tasks from different subjects can leave students with little time to rest, especially when they also have family responsibilities or other commitments.

Schools should therefore coordinate major assignments and avoid setting excessive weekend work. Teachers can give students clear priorities and enough time to complete important tasks during the week. A balanced approach supports learning while recognising that students need a life beyond homework.
hints: useful short assignments versus excessive workload
